name: Hyde Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Hyde Town Hall, on the train's {side}, opened in June 1885, four years after Hyde became a borough. It was built in red brick with stone dressings, with a domed clock tower, on the site of a cotton mill owner's house.

name: Apethorn Farmhouse
text: Your train passes near Apethorn Farmhouse, on the train's {side}, a cruck-framed farmhouse that tree-ring dating places between 1522 and 1542, a kind of building now rare in the region. Empty since the 1960s and damaged by fire in 1993, it was added to Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register.

name: Chadkirk Chapel
text: Your train passes near Chadkirk Chapel, on the train's {side}, whose oldest part, the half-timbered east end, probably dates from the 16th century. A chaplain is recorded here in 1347, and the 'kirk' in its name, a Scandinavian word for a church, suggests worship even earlier.

name: Elder Mill
text: Your train passes near the site of Elder Mill, on the train's {side}, a cotton-spinning mill beside the Peak Forest Canal. It was one of 104 mills bought by the Lancashire Cotton Corporation, which the Bank of England set up in 1929 to rescue the industry, and it passed to Courtaulds in 1964.

name: The Works Recording Studio
text: Your train passes near the site of The Works Recording Studio, on the train's {side}, which from 1998 to 2007 was in a Victorian rectory. Bands from Manchester's music scene recorded there, and in 2005 the American rapper Snoop Dogg turned up at 3am after a concert, with his musicians, bodyguards and a chef.

name: Reddish Vale
text: Your train passes Reddish Vale, on the train's {side}, a country park of woods and riverside meadows in the Tame valley. The line crosses it on a brick viaduct of 16 arches built in 1875, which a local witch is said to have cursed, along with anyone who counts its arches.

name: Brookfield Unitarian Church
text: Your train passes near Brookfield Unitarian Church, on the train's {side}, built between 1869 and 1871 for Richard Peacock of the locomotive builders Beyer, Peacock, who paid £12,000 for it. Its steeple has a peal of eight bells, each named after a member of his family, and he is buried in the mausoleum beside it.

name: Belle Vue Stadium
text: Your train passes near the site of Belle Vue Stadium, on the train's {side}, where the first greyhound race round an oval track in Britain was run on 24 July 1926. It was also home to the Belle Vue Aces speedway team, and its last race meeting was held in June 2020.

name: Marple Aqueduct
text: Your train passes near Marple Aqueduct, on the train's {side}, which carries the Peak Forest Canal across the River Goyt and is the highest aqueduct in England. Begun in 1795 and in use by 1800, it was nearly demolished after part of a wall collapsed in 1962, but was repaired instead.

name: St Martin's Church, Marple
text: Your train passes close to St Martin's Church, Marple, on the train's {side}, designed by J. D. Sedding and built in 1869 and 1870. Its chancel windows are stained glass from William Morris's company, with designs by Edward Burne-Jones, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Ford Madox Brown and Morris himself.

name: Mellor Mill
text: Your train passes near the site of Mellor Mill, on the train's {side}, a six-storey cotton mill built by Samuel Oldknow in 1793 beside the River Goyt. At its peak in 1804 it had 10,080 spindles and employed about 550 people; it burnt down in 1892, and its mill ponds are now known as the Roman Lakes.

name: Newton
text: Your train passes near Newton, on the train's {side}, a part of Hyde that runs in a narrow strip from the River Tame to Matley, between Hyde and Dukinfield. It was once a township of the Cheshire parish of Mottram-in-Longdendale.

name: St Paul's Church, Hyde
text: Your train passes close to St Paul's Church, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church in the Gothic Revival style built in 1853 and 1854. The land for it was given by Robert Ashton, a Unitarian who owned Hyde Print Works.

name: Godley Reservoir
text: Your train passes near Godley Reservoir, on the train's {side}, completed in 1851 as part of the Longdendale Chain, which brings drinking water from the River Etherow to Manchester. In 2016 a floating solar farm was built on it, at the time the largest of its kind in the UK.

name: Godley Hall Inn
text: Your train passes close to Godley Hall Inn, on the train's {side}, built as a house in 1718, the date on a door lintel, and a pub by 1830. It closed in 2020, and in 2021 permission was given to turn it back into a home.

name: Broadbottom Hall
text: Your train passes near Broadbottom Hall, on the train's {side}, a stone house dated 1680 by the inscription 'JW1680' over its door. It is L-shaped, with a two-storey porch, and inside it keeps timber-framed partitions of wattle and daub.

name: Stayley Hall
text: Your train passes near Stayley Hall, on the train's {side}, home of the Staley family, lords of the manor, and standing by the early 15th century. Built of timber on a knoll that was easy to defend, it was encased in local gritstone in the 17th century.

name: Mossley Hall
text: Your train passes close to Mossley Hall, on the train's {side}, built between 1861 and 1864 as a house for the Mayall family, who owned Bottoms' Mill on the east side of the railway. It cost more than £60,000, and in 1891 the new borough council bought it as its town hall for just £4,000.

name: Standedge Tunnel
text: Your train goes through Standedge Tunnel under the Pennines, a double-track bore opened in 1894. It runs beside two older single-track railway tunnels and a canal tunnel of 1811, the longest, deepest and highest canal tunnel in the UK, and all four are joined by cross-passages.

name: Middlewood Higher station
text: Your train passes the site of Middlewood Higher station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1879 on a line that crossed above this one, with steps down to a station below so passengers could change. It closed in 1960, but its bridge over this line still stands, and the old line is now the Middlewood Way path.

name: St Mary's Church, Disley
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Disley, on the train's {side}, on a hill above the village. It was begun as a chantry chapel for Sir Piers Legh of Lyme, consecrated as a parish church in 1558, and the weather vane on its tower once stood on Stockport's parish church.

name: Gritstone Trail
text: Your train passes close to the Gritstone Trail, on the train's {side}, a footpath of 35 miles that starts at Disley station and follows the most westerly hills of the Peak District to Mow Cop and Kidsgrove. Its waymarks show a footprint marked with a 'G'.

name: Hart Common
text: Your train passes near Hart Common, on the train's {side}, once one of the most rural hamlets of Westhoughton. It takes its name from the Hart family, whose small estate adjoined common land, and it is first recorded as a place name in 1541.

name: St James' Church, Daisy Hill
text: Your train passes near St James' Church, Daisy Hill, on the train's {side}, built of brick and terracotta between 1879 and 1881 to a design by the Lancaster architects Paley and Austin. Its cost of £6,500 was met by two sisters, and it is admired as a fine church built for little money.

name: Atherton Laburnum Rovers
text: Your train passes close to the ground of Atherton Laburnum Rovers, on the train's {side}, a football club started in 1956 as an under-14 team. It took its name from the playing fields of the Laburnum cotton mill, where it first played.

name: The Ellesmere
text: Your train passes close to The Ellesmere, on the train's {side}, a High Victorian Gothic building put up in the 1860s or 1870s as a pub for passengers at Walkden Stocks station next door. The station closed in 1954, and the old pub is now offices.

name: Wardley Hall
text: Your train passes near Wardley Hall, on the train's {side}, where a moat is recorded from at least 1292. The present house dates from the 16th century, though much rebuilt since, and it is now the home of the Catholic Bishop of Salford.

name: Station Road, Swinton
text: Your train passes near the site of Station Road, on the train's {side}, home of Swinton Rugby League Club from 1929 to 1992 and once one of the finest grounds in the game. Its record crowd was 44,621, for a Challenge Cup semi-final between Warrington and Wigan in 1951.

name: St Augustine's Church, Pendlebury
text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Church, Pendlebury, on the train's {side}, known as the 'Miners' Cathedral' for its great size in what was a coal-mining community. G. F. Bodley designed it, and it was built between 1871 and 1874, paid for by the Manchester banker Edward Stanley Heywood.

name: Agecroft Power Station
text: Your train passes near the site of Agecroft Power Station, on the train's {side}, which ran on coal from 1925 to 1993 and is now covered by Forest Bank prison. Agecroft Hall, a manor house that stood nearby, was taken down and shipped to Richmond, Virginia.

name: Wet Earth Colliery
text: Your train passes near the site of Wet Earth Colliery, on the train's {side}, now Clifton Country Park. Here between 1752 and 1756 James Brindley made water run uphill: a weir and a tunnel brought river water to a wheel that pumped the mine dry, and his scheme stayed in use for 170 years.

name: Kearsley Mill
text: Your train passes near Kearsley Mill, on the train's {side}, a cotton-spinning mill begun in 1905 and finished in March 1906 for the Kearsley Spinning Company. It is a near-complete example of an Edwardian mill, and textiles are still made and sent out from it.

name: St John the Evangelist's Church, Farnworth
text: Your train passes near St John the Evangelist's Church, Farnworth, on the train's {side}, built between 1824 and 1826 to a design by Thomas Hardwick, as a Commissioners' church. Paley and Austin added the chancel in 1873, and the tower lost its pinnacles in 1912.

name: Burnden Park
text: Your train passes near the site of Burnden Park, on the train's {side}, home of Bolton Wanderers from 1895 to 1997. It staged the replay of the 1901 FA Cup final, and L. S. Lowry painted its crowds in 'Going to the Match' in 1953.

name: Octagon Theatre
text: Your train passes near the Octagon Theatre, on the train's {side}, opened by Princess Margaret in November 1967, the first professional theatre built in the North West after the Second World War. Its auditorium is actually six-sided, but Reading already had a Hexagon Theatre.

name: Bolton Parish Church
text: Your train passes close to Bolton Parish Church, on the train's {side}, built between 1867 and 1871 and paid for by Peter Ormrod, a cotton spinner and banker. It is the fourth church on the site: pulling down the 15th-century one found pre-Norman carved stones beneath its tower.

name: Hall i' th' Wood
text: Your train passes near Hall i' th' Wood, on the train's {side}, an early 16th-century timber-framed manor house. Samuel Crompton lived in part of it in the 18th century and built the first spinning mule there, and William Lever restored it and gave it to Bolton, which runs it as a museum.

name: Turton Tower
text: Your train passes close to Turton Tower, on the train's {side}, which began as a stone pele tower, probably in the early 15th century. Cruck-framed buildings were added in the 16th century, and the house was altered again in Elizabethan and early Victorian times.

name: St Peter's Church, Darwen
text: Your train passes close to St Peter's Church, Darwen, on the train's {side}, built between 1827 and 1829 to a design by Thomas Rickman and Henry Hutchinson. During the Second World War a young Don Estelle sang in its choir; he later appeared in 'It Ain't Half Hot Mum'.

name: Ewood Park
text: Your train passes near Ewood Park, on the train's {side}, home of Blackburn Rovers since 1890. Football was played here from 1881, and the ground now holds 31,367, with a stand named after Jack Walker, a local industrialist and supporter of the club.
